who.p: Managed care contracts govern every dollar a health system earns from commercial payers — yet most contracting teams still read them in PDF, compare terms manually, and build negotiation prep in spreadsheets. padu.h2: How Murphi.ai Reads Every Contract Clause
padu.sub: Every clause in every payer contract is scored using the PADU+ framework — a four-tier assessment model developed specifically for managed care contract analysis. Each clause is rated Preferred, Acceptable, Discouraged, or Unacceptable, linked to the exact source text, and compared against your internal manuals and payer policies.

prose.text: PADU+ gives your contracting team a clear, consistent language for evaluating contract quality. A
clause is the gold standard your negotiators should be pushing toward. An
clause introduces risk or unfavorable terms worth challenging. An
clause is a hard stop — it must be removed or renegotiated before execution. Every rating is traceable to the contract page and line.

rows.title: Preferred — Clause is the gold standard for your organization
rows.desc: Contract language is optimal — it fully aligns with your operational standards, protects your reimbursement, and reflects best-practice contract terms. Your negotiators should use Preferred clauses as the benchmark to anchor future renewals.
rows.example: e.g. "Payment within 30 days of clean electronic claim receipt, with interest accruing on delayed payments" — Preferred: tight timeline plus interest provision.

rows.title: Acceptable — Clause meets baseline requirements
rows.desc: The term is not optimal but meets the minimum threshold your organization can operate within. No immediate action needed, but these clauses should be tracked as targets for improvement at the next renewal cycle.
rows.example: e.g. "Payment within 45 days of clean claim receipt" — Acceptable: within state prompt-pay law, but not as favorable as a 30-day term.

rows.title: Discouraged — Clause introduces financial or operational risk
rows.desc: The term is unfavorable and creates meaningful exposure — reimbursement risk, operational burden, or compliance complexity. Your managed care team should push back on Discouraged clauses before signing and prioritize removing them at renewal.
rows.example: e.g. "Payer reserves the right to retrospective audit up to 36 months" — Discouraged: extends beyond industry norm of 12–24 months; creates prolonged financial uncertainty.

rows.title: Unacceptable — Clause must be removed or renegotiated
rows.desc: The term is a hard stop. It violates your operational policies, creates unacceptable financial risk, conflicts with a regulatory requirement, or gives the payer unrestricted unilateral power. Do not execute a contract with an Unacceptable clause unresolved.
rows.example: e.g. "Payer may amend reimbursement rates at any time without prior notice to Provider" — Unacceptable: no rate stability, no notice, no recourse.

rows.title: PLUS Extensions — Context tags beyond the four-tier score
rows.desc: Each PADU rating carries additional context tags: Negotiation Leverage, Reimbursement Risk, Rate Opportunity, Compliance Gap, Manual Conflict — so your team knows not just how a clause scores, but what to do with it next.
rows.example: e.g. A Discouraged audit clause tagged "Negotiation Leverage" signals it's a strong trade in renewal — offer to accept 24 months in exchange for a rate improvement.

analyzer.h2: The Payer Contract Analyzer — In Action
analyzer.sub: Upload a contract, select a finding, and see the clause evidence and comparison instantly. Add negotiation notes without leaving the screen.

findings.summary: Payer may amend rates at any time without advance notice — no rate stability guaranteed.
findings.evidence: Payer reserves the right to modify, amend, or replace applicable fee schedules and reimbursement rates at its sole discretion at any time, with or without prior notice to Provider.
findings.comparison: Operations Manual Section 5.2 requires a minimum 90-day advance notice for any reimbursement rate change. Aetna Provider Manual Section 3.1 states changes are communicated 30 days in advance. This contract clause grants the payer unlimited unilateral rate-change authority with zero notice obligation.
findings.note: UNACCEPTABLE — do not execute without removing this clause. Request: rates locked for the contract term with a minimum 90-day written notice for any amendment, and a right to terminate if proposed rates are below our cost threshold.

findings.summary: Payer can materially alter contract terms by posting updates to its website with no direct notice.
findings.evidence: Payer may modify the terms of this Agreement, including but not limited to covered services, reimbursement schedules, and administrative requirements, by posting notice of such modifications to the Payer's provider portal. Continued submission of claims by Provider shall constitute acceptance of such modifications.
findings.comparison: State insurance code requires written notice of material contract changes to contracted providers. Operations Manual Section 2.4 prohibits acceptance of contract modifications by conduct. Claim submission cannot legally constitute contract acceptance under the doctrine of mutual assent.
findings.note: UNACCEPTABLE — website-posting plus claim-submission-as-acceptance is legally suspect and operationally unworkable. Require all material modifications to be in writing, signed, and subject to a 60-day opt-out window.

findings.summary: Payer retains right to audit and recoup payments for up to 36 months — double the industry norm.
findings.evidence: Payer reserves the right to conduct retrospective claim audits and to recoup any amounts determined to be overpaid for a period not to exceed thirty-six (36) months from the date of original payment.
findings.comparison: Operations Manual Section 12.3 establishes a 12-month internal standard for retrospective audit exposure. BCBS Provider Manual references 12–24 months as standard audit periods. This 36-month window extends recoupment risk significantly beyond both internal policy and industry practice.
findings.note: DISCOURAGED — push back at renewal. Offer 18 months as a counter. If payer insists on 36 months, require a corresponding 36-month timely filing window and interest on delayed payments.

findings.summary: Contract sets a 90-day filing deadline — below our 120-day operational standard.
findings.evidence: Provider shall submit all claims for covered services within ninety (90) days of the date of service. Claims submitted after this period shall be considered untimely and may be denied without right of appeal.
findings.comparison: Operations Manual Section 7.1 requires 120-day timely filing windows for all commercial contracts to accommodate downstream documentation and coding workflows. State law does not mandate a specific window. Industry standard for commercial contracts is 90–180 days.
findings.note: DISCOURAGED — 90 days creates operational risk for complex cases. Request 120 days to align with internal policy. If denied, flag all encounters over 75 days for priority billing review.

findings.summary: 30-day electronic, 45-day paper payment terms — meets state prompt payment law and internal standard.
findings.evidence: Payer shall remit payment for clean claims within thirty (30) days of receipt for electronic submissions and forty-five (45) days for paper submissions, in accordance with applicable state prompt payment requirements.
findings.comparison: State prompt payment law mandates electronic claims paid within 30 days. Operations Manual Section 8.2 sets 30-day internal target for commercial payers. This contract aligns with both. Payer Provider Manual confirms same standard.
findings.note: ACCEPTABLE — meets baseline. At next renewal, push for 21-day electronic payment to move toward Preferred status. Also seek interest on late payments beyond 30 days.

findings.summary: Payer owes 1.5% monthly interest on clean claims paid beyond 30 days — fully Preferred.
findings.evidence: In the event Payer fails to remit payment on a clean claim within thirty (30) days of receipt, Payer shall pay interest on the outstanding balance at a rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month from the day following the due date until paid in full.
findings.comparison: Operations Manual Section 8.3 identifies interest-on-late-payments as a target provision for all contract renewals. Aetna Provider Manual does not include this provision in its standard agreement — this is a negotiated enhancement above the standard. State prompt payment law imposes only 10% annual interest; this contract exceeds that floor.
findings.note: PREFERRED — retain in all renewals. Use this clause as a benchmark when negotiating other Aetna agreements for the same service lines.
